c.tagline: Brazil's Afro-Bahian soul — cobbled colonial squares, drum-driven streets, and Atlantic beaches.

taxi.fareNote: City taxis are metered, but for the airport run and longer trips agreeing a flat fare first is common; ride-hailing (Uber/99) is usually cheaper and easier for visitors.

emergency.note: Dial 190 for police, 192 for the SAMU ambulance service, and 193 for the fire brigade.

avoid.reason: Cidade Baixa & streets around Pelourinho at night; street crime

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed colonial old town in the upper city, a maze of pastel 17th–18th-century mansions, baroque churches and cobbled squares alive with capoeira, drumming and Afro-Bahian culture; best for first-timers who want to be steps from the landmarks, though it quiets down late.

A lively beachfront district around the Farol da Barra lighthouse and Porto da Barra beach, packed with hostels, bars, shops and the Barra–Ondina Carnival circuit; a convenient, walkable base with sand and sunsets on the doorstep.

Salvador's bohemian nightlife and dining hub, an old fishing quarter turned buzzing strip of bars, live music, seafood spots and the famous acarajé of Dinha and Cira; suits travelers who want to eat and go out where locals do.
A calm oceanfront neighborhood just south of Barra with beachfront hotels, the aquarium and easy access to the center; good for a quieter seaside stay within reach of the action.

A traditional far-eastern beach neighborhood rich in Afro-Brazilian music, folklore and coconut-lined sands near the lighthouse and lagoon; relaxed and local, popular with families and those wanting resort-style calm away from downtown.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water rather than tap.

transit.hours: The Metrô runs roughly 5am to midnight with trains every 5–8 minutes; buses stop around midnight and restart near 4:30–5am, so late-night trips fall to taxis or ride-hailing.
transit.pay: Tap a rechargeable SalvadorCARD on the Metrô, city buses and BRT; a single Metrô ride is about R$4.10 (~$0.75) and a metro+bus transfer within about 2 hours runs around R$5.60. The historic Elevador Lacerda linking the upper and lower city costs just R$0.15.

food.name: Acaraje
food.desc: Black-eyed pea fritter deep-fried in dende palm oil, split and stuffed with vatapa, caruru, dried shrimp and pepper sauce. Sold by baianas in white lace.

places.name: Acaraje da Dinha
places.note: Institution at Largo de Santana; queues into the night for acaraje, abara and vatapa.

places.name: Acaraje da Cira
places.note: Rival stand at Largo da Mariquita, equally famous and open late by the bars.

places.name: Mercado do Peixe
places.note: Fish market strip where acaraje stalls sit beside beer tables until dawn.

food.name: Moqueca baiana
food.desc: Fish or shrimp simmered in a clay pot with coconut milk, dende oil, tomato, onion and coriander, served with rice, farofa and pirao.

places.name: Ki-Mukeka
places.note: Specialist moqueca house locals rate for over a decade of consistent clay-pot stews.

places.name: Sorriso da Dada
places.note: Chef Dada's celebrated Bahian kitchen in the old town; fish moqueca is the signature.

places.name: Restaurante Yemanja
places.note: Large seafood classic on the coast road, long a first stop for visitors wanting moqueca.

food.name: Vatapa and caruru
food.desc: Vatapa is a creamy puree of bread, shrimp, peanuts, coconut milk and dende; caruru adds okra. Eaten inside acaraje or spooned over rice.

places.name: Casa de Tereza
places.note: Colonial house doing refined Bahian cooking; vatapa and bobo among the standouts.

places.name: Acaraje da Dinha
places.note: Order vatapa and caruru as a plate if you want them without the fritter.

places.name: Sorriso da Dada
places.note: Traditional accompaniments made in the old Bahian way alongside the mains.

food.name: Bobo de camarao
food.desc: Shrimp in a velvety puree of cassava, coconut milk and dende oil, richer and thicker than moqueca, always with white rice.

places.name: Casa de Tereza
places.note: Restored colonial building; bobo de camarao is one of the house classics.

places.name: Sorriso da Dada
places.note: Signature bobo de camarao from one of Salvador's best known cooks.

places.name: Restaurante Yemanja
places.note: Dependable version on a long menu of Bahian seafood.

food.name: Xinxim de galinha
food.desc: Chicken braised with dried shrimp, ground peanuts and cashews, ginger and dende oil, a dish tied to Candomble offerings to Oxum.

places.name: Sorriso da Dada
places.note: Keeps the Afro-Bahian repertoire, xinxim included, on a menu of old recipes.

places.name: Casa de Tereza
places.note: Bahian cooking with African and European roots; ask for the day's traditional plate.

places.name: Restaurante Yemanja
places.note: Broad Bahian carte that runs beyond seafood into poultry classics.

food.name: Cocada and other doces baianos
food.desc: Chewy coconut sweets in white or burnt-sugar brown, plus bolinho de estudante and cocada de banana, sold from trays across the old city.

places.name: Mercado Modelo
places.note: Historic market by the Lacerda lift stacked with cocadas, sweets and cachaca.

places.name: Feira de Sao Joaquim
places.note: Sprawling working market; the cheapest and freshest sweets and dende oil in town.

places.name: Terreiro de Jesus
places.note: Square where tray vendors sell cocada, tapioca and peanut sweets all day.

food.name: Caipirinha
food.desc: Cachaca crushed with lime and sugar over ice; in Bahia it is often made with passionfruit, cajá or tangerine instead of lime.

places.name: Mercado do Peixe
places.note: Plastic tables and cold caipirinhas beside the fish stalls, busiest after dark.

places.name: Mercado Modelo
places.note: Upstairs bars mix caipirinhas with bay views; ground floor sells artisan cachaca.

places.name: Bars of Largo da Mariquita
places.note: Nightlife heart of the city, where a caipirinha follows the acaraje stands.

food.name: Sucos of Bahian fruit
food.desc: Fresh juices of cajá, umbu, graviola, cupuacu and acerola, plus chilled coconut water straight from the shell at every beach kiosk.

places.name: Feira de Sao Joaquim
places.note: Fruit stalls and juice counters showing the full range of northeastern fruit.

places.name: Barraca kiosks of Praia do Porto da Barra
places.note: Beachfront huts pressing juice and cracking green coconuts all day.

places.name: Mercado Modelo
places.note: Juice bars inside the market for cajá and umbu between shopping stalls.

landmarks: Pelourinho Historic Center
A UNESCO World Heritage colonial quarter of cobblestone streets and vividly colored facades, the beating heart of Afro-Brazilian culture.
Elevador Lacerda
A dramatic Art Deco public elevator connecting the upper and lower city, offering one of Salvador's most iconic skyline and bay views.
Church and Convent of São Francisco
A baroque masterpiece whose interior is covered in gold leaf, considered one of the most opulent churches in Brazil.
Salvador Cathedral (Sé)
A grand 17th-century Jesuit cathedral facade anchoring Praça da Sé, a centerpiece of Salvador's historic skyline.
Igreja do Bonfim (Church of Nosso Senhor do Bonfim)
Salvador's most beloved pilgrimage church, famous for its colorful wish ribbons tied to the gates and its role in Bahian folk religion.
Farol da Barra (Barra Lighthouse)
A historic lighthouse atop a 16th-century fort where the bay meets the ocean, famous for spectacular sunsets over the Atlantic.
Mercado Modelo
A historic waterfront market building turned crafts bazaar, packed with Bahian art, capoeira demonstrations, and bay views.
Forte de São Marcelo
A rare circular sea fort floating just offshore in the Bay of All Saints, one of Brazil's most unusual colonial fortifications.
Terreiro de Jesus
A lively colonial square ringed by baroque churches and a beautiful fountain, the traditional gathering place of the old city.
Bay of All Saints (Baía de Todos os Santos)
The vast, island-dotted bay framing the city, best photographed at sunset from the Elevador Lacerda or Barra lighthouse.

train.note: Brazil has no intercity passenger rail and Salvador is no exception - the city has a two-line metro but nothing that leaves the region. All long-distance travel is by coach or plane. The nearest passenger railway is the Vale ore-line train far to the south between Belo Horizonte and Vitória.

bus.note: No international coaches. The Rodoviária on Avenida ACM is the hub, with Águia Branca, Cometa and Gontijo running to Recife (about 20 hours), Rio de Janeiro (28) and Belo Horizonte; book through ClickBus (https://www.clickbus.com.br/) or Buser (https://www.buser.com.br/). For most of these routes flying is far quicker.

intl.to: Mar Grande, Itaparica Island (Brazil) - ~35 min from the Terminal Náutico
intl.op: catamaran and lancha operators — tickets at the terminal

intl.to: Bom Despacho, Itaparica (Brazil) - car ferry from São Joaquim, ~50 min

ferry.note: There are no international sailings. The Bay of All Saints crossings are genuinely useful transport rather than sightseeing: the São Joaquim car ferry carries vehicles over to Itaparica and cuts hours off the drive south toward Morro de São Paulo, while the small lanchas from the Terminal Náutico beside the Mercado Modelo are the quick foot-passenger option. Both can be suspended in rough weather, and the catamarans to Morro de São Paulo take about two hours.

half.name: Praia do Forte
half.blurb: A beach village about an hour and a half north has calm natural reef pools and a sea turtle conservation project, Projeto Tamar.

half.name: Itaparica Island
half.blurb: A ferry about 50 minutes away reaches an island of colonial-era buildings, mangroves, and beaches across the Bay of All Saints.

half.name: Cachoeira
half.blurb: A colonial river town about an hour and a half inland preserves Baroque churches and a strong Afro-Brazilian religious and craft tradition.

full.name: Morro de São Paulo
full.blurb: A catamaran ride of about two hours reaches this car-free island village of sandy paths, cliffside pousadas, and palm-lined beaches.
